workingTitle: Two quasars heated a vast bubble in the young universe
publicationStatus: Peer-reviewed Nature Astronomy article published 18 November 2026
coreFacts: The dual quasar system J1549+1245 is at redshift 2.37, seen about 2.8 billion years after the Big Bang.
A thermal Sunyaev-Zel'dovich flux decrement detects localized hot gas at 6 sigma.
The inferred thermal energy is (9.7 ± 1.6) × 10^60 ergs.
That energy is 3.6 times the expected hot-gas energy of a 10^13-solar-mass dark matter halo and at least 0.6 percent of the quasar system's lifetime energy output.
Additional hot gas is detected on roughly 100-kiloparsec scales at 5 sigma, with broader 100 to 600 kiloparsec evidence interpreted more cautiously.

sources.label: Excess intergalactic heating around a dual quasar system 2.8 Gyr after the Big Bang

sourceStatus: Primary peer-reviewed article and full author manuscript read; secondary corroboration unnecessary.
caveats: The millimeter decrement directly measures electron pressure, while the attribution of excess heating to quasar-driven winds is an inference supported by energy comparisons and simulations.
The larger-scale gas is lower-significance evidence and may not all share the same origin.
